stem: A 23-year-old man is being evaluated for progressive muscle weakness and difficulty ambulating for the past 2 years.  He has had myoclonic epilepsy since adolescence and progressive vision and hearing impairment.  Physical examination shows intermittent myoclonic jerks, proximal muscle weakness, ataxic gait, decreased visual acuity, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.  A muscle biopsy with modified trichrome staining shows red muscle fibers with irregular, blotchy margins.  Assuming an unaffected partner, which of the following is the most likely probability of this patient passing the disease to his offspring?​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​
explanation:
This patient with progressive encephalomyopathy and blotchy, irregular red muscle fibers (red ragged fibers) most likely has a mitochondrial disorder.  Mitochondrial disorders are caused by mutations that impair mitochondrial function.  They typically affect tissues with high energy demands, most notably skeletal muscle and the nervous system, due to impaired oxidative phosphorylation.  Skeletal muscle involvement leads to the characteristic red-ragged fibers on Gomori trichrome staining, which reflect subsarcolemmal and intermyofibrillar accumulations of abnormal mitochondria.

Although most mitochondrial proteins are encoded by nuclear DNA, mitochondria possess their own DNA (mtDNA), a circular genome that encodes 13 essential proteins for the electron transport chain, along with rRNAs and tRNAs.  Mitochondrial disorders can therefore arise from mutations in either mtDNA or nuclear DNA.

This patient's symptoms are particularly suggestive of myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF), a syndrome that is caused by mutations in mtDNA.  Other common syndromes associated with mtDNA mutations include MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes) and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (severe and permanent visual loss).

mtDNA mutations follow a maternal inheritance pattern.  Mitochondrial DNA is normally transmitted exclusively from the mother to all offspring, as paternal mitochondria do not usually survive in the ovum following fertilization.  Therefore, the probability of this male patient passing the mutation to his offspring is 0%.  In contrast, females with mtDNA mutations pass them to all offspring, though clinical expression varies due to heteroplasmy (the proportion of mutated to normal mitochondria in each cell) (Choice A).

(Choices B, C, and D)  Mitochondrial disorders caused by mutations in nuclear DNA follow Mendelian inheritance and can be transmitted in an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked manner.  However, this patient's characteristic features of MERRF make an mtDNA mutation more likely.

Educational objective:Mitochondrial disorders can be caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is inherited exclusively from the mother.  MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers), MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes), and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy are specific mitochondrial disorders caused by mtDNA mutations.​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​
